aspects.says: A cleaning action that refers to its object, such as a lambda reading a field, keeps the object reachable from the Cleaner, so it is never cleaned.
basis: section:A Cleaner Runs After a Collection Finds Its Object, So close() Is the Release You Can Count On

aspects.says: A Cleaner's action runs only after a collection finds its object unreachable, never if no collection happens; close() through the Cleanable releases at once and only once.
basis: section:A Cleaner Runs After a Collection Finds Its Object, So close() Is the Release You Can Count On

aspects.says: Each collector puts the cost of the same workload somewhere else: G1 in short pauses, Serial and Parallel in longer ones (Parallel in full collections when the heap is tight), single-generation ZGC in allocation stalls that no Pause line shows.
basis: section:Each Collector Puts the Cost Somewhere: Pauses, Stalls or CPU

aspects.says: An object is alive when a path of references leads to it from a root; nothing counts references, so an unreachable cycle is collected.
basis: section:A Young Collection Costs What Survives, Not What Was Allocated
aspects.reason: the run shows it in one line; both code practices rest on it, but a cycle on its own leaves the reader nothing to write

aspects.says: Soft references survive collections while the heap has room (HotSpot keeps recently used ones longer) and are all cleared when a collection can't free enough, so a soft cache empties at once.
basis: section:A Soft Cache Survives Collections While There Is Room, and Empties When an Allocation Doesn't Fit

aspects.says: System.gc() asks for a collection: on G1 and Parallel it is a full stop-the-world collection, and with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC it does nothing.
basis: section:System.gc() Is a Request, and JVM Flags Decide What It Does

aspects.says: A WeakHashMap entry goes only when nothing else reaches its key; a value that refers to its key, or an interned literal key, keeps the entry.
basis: section:A WeakHashMap Entry Goes Only When Nothing Else Reaches Its Key

aspects.says: A WeakHashMap entry disappears after the reference handler queues the cleared reference, not at the moment of the collection.
basis: section:A WeakHashMap Entry Goes Only When Nothing Else Reaches Its Key
aspects.reason: the timing belongs to the JDK's reference handler; the practice's tests absorb it by waiting, and nothing the reader writes changes it

aspects.says: A young collection copies only what is still alive, so short-lived garbage is cheap and objects that outlive a few collections cost copying, promotion and old-generation marking.
basis: section:A Young Collection Costs What Survives, Not What Was Allocated
